name: Keeping Health Information Out of AI Tools
title: Keeping Health Information Out of AI Tools
answer: Student health information is among the most sensitive data a school holds, and typing a diagnosis, medication, or injury into a general AI chat tool shares that record with a company the school has no agreement with. The safe habit is to describe needs in general terms, such as asking for activities for a student with limited use of one arm, so no private information leaves the school. When a plan truly depends on medical details, the nurse and family belong in the conversation.

crumbs.name: Arts, Music, Physical Education, and Health

sections.body: This idea is about keeping student health information out of AI tools that the school has no agreement with. Records kept by a school nurse are generally part of a student's education records under FERPA, so a teacher who types a student's diagnosis, medication, or injury into a general chat tool has effectively shared that record with an outside company. The problem it solves is the accidental disclosure of sensitive health data through ordinary lesson planning. PE and health teachers run into this risk more than most, because their work often involves adapting activities to a student's condition or answering personal health questions. The name removal habit described earlier in the book is the same instinct applied here, and it prevents a small convenience from turning into a privacy breach.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, a teacher describes the need rather than the student. A PE teacher planning an adapted activity can ask for activities suitable for a student with limited use of one arm instead of naming the student and their diagnosis, and the result is just as useful. A health teacher who wants help responding to a student's personal question can frame the request in general terms rather than repeating the student's details. The text does not give separate grade band guidance for this idea, so the same approach applies across year levels. When a plan depends on medical details, the nurse and family should be part of the conversation rather than the AI tool.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure, or finding for this idea, and it does not carry an evidence label. It rests on practice and on the FERPA framing set out in Chapter 3 rather than on research. The claim that the general-terms approach produces an equally useful result is presented as the book's practical guidance, not as a measured outcome.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are clear in the text. Health details that identify a student should stay out of the tool, and the decision about what counts as identifying information stays with the teacher. When an adapted plan depends on medical details, the nurse and family make those decisions, not the AI tool. The teacher also carries the responsibility for recognising when a request has drifted into sensitive territory, which is exactly the mistake the name removal habit is meant to prevent. Nothing here is legal advice, and the text describes practice rather than setting out legal rules.
